newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Courtaulds guardedly upbeat on H2.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Courtaulds guardedly upbeat on H2.

text.p: Chemicals company Courtaulds Plc said on Wednesday that momentum would continue into the second half of the year, but it was wary of the possible impact of a strong pound and uncertainty over its viscose operations.

"You can assume the momentum of the first half (will continue), with two areas of uncertainty, viscose and a little concern about the strength of sterling," Gordon Campbell, chief executive of Courtaulds told Reuters in a telephone interview.
Courtaulds earlier announced that first half pretax profits had fallen to 64.0 million stg from 67.8 million previously.
This was at the low end of analysts' expectations but shares in the company firmed anyway, gaining 5p to 429p by 0945 GMT, as it paid a dividend of 4.45p per share, up from 4.3p last time.

Courtaulds said that there was underlying growth in all its key markets and that the group was better positioned now than has been the case for some time. It added that profits in its core businesses had improved in the first half.
The firm said that a poor performance from its acrylics and viscose operations depressed overall group profits and noted that it had seen little improvement in viscose.

"The acrylics market has turned around and we have seen progressive improvement in the last six months. I can't say the same for viscose -- in the last month or so we have seen an improvement in the order book but prices in viscose and hence the margins are still lousy," Campbell told Reuters.
He said that the firm was trying to raise prices on the back of the stronger order book, but added that it really now depended on how the market responds.
The other area of mild concern for Courtaulds has been the recent strengthening of the pound, which recently hit four-year highs versus the dollar and a 30-month peak on the mark.
"If the strength of sterling to the dollar continues then it is going to make margins tougher," said Campbell.
One of the brighter spots for the company was the performance of Tencel, a man-made material derived from wood-pulp, which admirers say offers considerable advantages over viscose and cotton.

Turnover in fibres and chemicals was flat at 437 million stg compared with 439 million at the halfway stage last year, but sales of Tencel in the first six months were nearly double those of a year ago, said the company.
"We can't see any growth between now and next year (in Tencel) because we are at capacity and we can't sell anymore until the new facility comes onstream in the UK," Campbell told Reuters.
Courtaulds plans its third Tencel plant to be located in Grimsby in northern England and it is on schedule for commissioning towards the end of 1997.
Campbell said the company also plans to start manufacturing Tencel in Asia, which is one of the main driving areas of the textiles industry, and reckons that should be onstream before the year 2000.
"We expect to make a decision in the next few months as to where it is going to be," said Campbell.
Some analysts have suggested that a deterioration in Courtaulds' cash performance and the potential for increased demand for Tencel might prompt the firm to make a rights issue.
Campbell, however, dismissed the idea, "We have no plans for a rights issue, we beleive that we can fund our organic growth from our own resources."
